summary: Defines the Network Control Protocol for setting up and configuring the Xerox Network Systems Internet Datagram Protocol over PPP. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: The rules for a link to agree to carry traffic from an old Xerox networking system.

subtitle: Using Xerox's network protocol over point-to-point links

tldr.problem: PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) provides a standard way to transmit data over serial links, but it needed to support many different network-layer protocols. Xerox Network Systems (XNS) was a proprietary network protocol used in some corporate networks, and organizations needed a way to run it over PPP links.
tldr.mechanism: XNSCP (XNS IDP Control Protocol) follows the same pattern as PPP's Link Control Protocol. It negotiates connection parameters and configures the XNS IDP protocol module on both ends of the link. XNS IDP datagrams are encapsulated in PPP frames using a specific protocol type identifier (hex 0025).
tldr.outcome: XNSCP allowed organizations with XNS networks to use PPP for point-to-point connections. The RFC is Historic because XNS itself is obsolete; most organizations have migrated to TCP/IP and Ethernet.

today: RFC 1764 is Historic. Xerox Network Systems is an obsolete network protocol. XNS was used in some corporate networks in the 1980s and 1990s but has been completely displaced by TCP/IP. This RFC is retained as a historical reference for anyone maintaining legacy systems that may still use XNS over PPP.

sections.title: PPP and Network Protocols
sections.content:
PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) is a standard method for transmitting data over serial point-to-point links, such as dial-up modems or leased lines. It has three main components: a method for encapsulating different types of datagrams, a Link Control Protocol (LCP) for negotiating and testing the link itself, and a family of Network Control Protocols for configuring specific network-layer protocols.

Before any actual data can be transmitted over a PPP link, the two endpoints must negotiate connection parameters using LCP packets. After the link is established, they must use a protocol-specific Network Control Protocol to enable and configure whichever network-layer protocol they want to use (IP, IPX, XNS, AppleTalk, or others).
sections.eli5: PPP is a standard way for two computers to talk over a serial cable. But first they have to agree on what language to use at the network layer. XNSCP is the agreement for using an old Xerox network protocol.

sections.title: XNSCP Configuration
sections.content:
XNSCP (XNS IDP Control Protocol) is the Network Control Protocol for establishing and configuring the Xerox Network Systems Internet Datagram Protocol over a PPP link. It uses the exact same packet exchange mechanism as LCP, but with protocol-specific modifications.

XNSCP packets are identified by a PPP protocol type field value of hex 8025. The protocol uses the same packet types as LCP: Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, Configure-Reject, Terminate-Request, and Terminate-Ack. However, XNSCP has no Configuration Options (unlike some other Network Control Protocols), so negotiation is straightforward: each end simply confirms that it is ready to enable XNS IDP.

XNSCP packets may not be exchanged until PPP has reached the Network-Layer Protocol phase, which occurs after LCP negotiation is complete and any authentication and link quality determination procedures have finished.
sections.eli5: XNSCP is just LCP adapted for XNS. Both sides say 'I agree to speak XNS' and then they can start sending XNS data.

sections.title: Sending Data
sections.content:
Once XNSCP has negotiated successfully and reached the Opened state, XNS IDP datagrams can be sent over the PPP link. Each datagram is encapsulated in the Information field of a PPP frame, with the protocol type field set to hex 0025 to indicate that the frame contains an XNS IDP datagram.

The maximum length of an XNS IDP datagram transmitted over PPP is equal to the maximum size of PPP's Information field. Since XNS IDP has no standard fragmentation and reassembly mechanism, PPP links supporting XNS IDP MUST allow at least 576 octets (bytes) in the Information field. This ensures compatibility with systems that generate larger datagrams and expect them to traverse a network without being broken apart.
sections.eli5: Once both sides agree, XNS datagrams can flow across the link. Each one is wrapped in a PPP frame, and the link must be able to handle messages at least 576 bytes long.
